extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media researchers, students, and general readers interested in media ethics and news quality
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for identifying and understanding 'churnalism' — news copy produced from press releases or other sources with little original reporting or fact-checking. Useful for evaluating news articles' originality, sourcing, and susceptibility to PR influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — low-quality or unoriginal news produced by paraphrasing other sources or press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Churnalism is the production of low-quality or unoriginal news articles, generally by paraphrasing other sources or press releases to avoid the need for time-consuming research or fact-checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core definitional criterion: look for paraphrase of press releases/other sources and minimal original reporting or investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of reporting / provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story is original reporting produced by reporters or derived from other sources/press releases (e.g., Cardiff study: 80% of stories in Britain's quality press were not original; only 12% generated by reporters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate provenance: who generated the story (staff reporter, wire service, PR), and whether primary reporting was conducted. Low originality indicates churnalism and reduced quality/accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of press releases as primary source
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that paraphrase or largely reproduce press releases (or agency copy) rather than relying on independent reporting or additional sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree to which the article depends on PR-provided text; heavy reliance suggests churnalism. Note the economic/structural link: many local papers and trade magazines rely on PR-provided stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking and research rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoidance of time-consuming research or fact-checking (i.e., processing incoming copy instead of verifying claims) is a hallmark of churnalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for evidence of verification, multiple independent sources, and corroboration. Lack of fact-checking increases susceptibility to manipulation and distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed/urgency versus quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritization of getting stories up fast (editorial emphasis on being first) that undermines quality — e.g., BBC guide: 'Get the story up as fast as you can ... We encourage a sense of urgency—we want to be first.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider editorial pressures and timelines; urgent publishing at the expense of checks is correlated with churnalism. Balance between speed and verification should be assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Token localisation or minimal added reporting ('odd local quote')
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding minor local touches such as 'the odd local quote' to pre-existing copy rather than conducting substantive local reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat token additions as indicators the article was 'processed' rather than reported; they are insufficient to transform PR copy into original journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to manipulation and distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Churnalism results in a reduction of quality and accuracy, as the articles are open to manipulation and distortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether reliance on secondary/PR sources introduced bias, spin, or factual distortions; evaluate the presence of unchallenged claims that mirror PR messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and resource drivers (staffing, revenue pressures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understaffed newsrooms, cuts in advertising revenue, and reduced resources lead to increased churnalism because outlets lack capacity for original news-gathering and checking sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider organizational context (staff numbers, budget cuts, local vs national outlets) when judging whether churnalism is likely or excusable; structural causes explain prevalence but do not excuse lack of verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on public relations / PR influence
rubrics_metrics.description: A relationship between the number of PR staff and journalists unemployed; local and trade publications commonly rely on stories brought to them by public relations representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine source diversity and whether PR actors are primary content providers; heavy PR-sourced content flags potential churnalism and conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement via text-matching / percent 'derived churn' (tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of automated tools (e.g., churnalism.com) that compare article text against a database of known press releases to determine what percentage of content is derived churn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply similarity/detection tools to quantify overlap with press releases; consider tool limitations and contextual interpretation (not all overlap is bad, but high percentages indicate churnalism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Writethroughs, plagiarism and unattributed reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices such as 'writethroughs' (extensive reuse of another author's text) and plagiarism are labelled churnalism when material is reused without proper attribution or original contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for attribution, quotation, and transformative contribution. Unattributed reuse of another author's text is a negative quality indicator and may amount to plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oversight, monitoring and corrective mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of watchdog programs (e.g., Media Watch), tools, and organisations (Sunlight Foundation, Media Standards Trust) in exposing churnalism, plagiarism and media bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether editorial oversight, fact-checking desks, or external watchdogs are active; their presence mitigates churnalism and provides corrective pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate over normalisation versus alarmism
rubrics_metrics.description: Differing views on churnalism's severity: some see a terminal decline in journalism quality, others argue there was never a 'golden age' and some churn is normal/inevitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating instances of churn, contextualise them within debates over media practice and historical norms; distinguish occasional, explainable reuse from systematic decline in reporting standards.
